rationale: The printed entry defines 'garden' as a planted stand of trees, i.e., a grouping of nations, and anchors it to Ezekiel 31:9. Within Ezekiel 31 the identification is essentially self-decoding: Assyria is a cedar (31:3), the 'trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God' envy him (31:9), those same trees descend to Sheol with the slain (31:16-17), and Ezekiel closes with the explicit key, 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude' (31:18). Trees that envy, are comforted, and go down to the grave are kings and nations, not botanical paradise flora; the garden of God in this passage is therefore the collective planting of nation-trees. The tree=nation premise is independently decoded in Scripture itself (Daniel 4:20-22; Ezekiel 17:22-24; Hosea 10:1; Romans 11), so the derivation garden=grouping of nation-trees adds only one small, natural step. The strongest counter — garden as Eden/paradise, the place of God's presence, with the nation-trees merely compared hyperbolically to paradise splendor — must add an extra layer (kings 'likened to' Eden's trees) and still cannot comfortably explain why heathen empires like Assyria and Egypt stand 'in the garden of God' if the garden denotes unbroken communion with God, nor why 'trees of Eden' are found in Sheol. No supplied text is better explained by the counter than by the book. The entry's core therefore stands as the best-supported explanation of the cited evidence; the chapter's further Isaiah applications are more contestable but are elaborations beyond the printed entry.
book_core_identification: A garden, as a biblical symbol, is a planted stand of trees, and since a tree symbolizes a nation, a garden symbolizes a grouping of nations — demonstrated from Ezekiel 31:9,18, where the 'trees of Eden in the garden of God' are decoded by Ezekiel himself as Pharaoh, Assyria, and their multitudes.
book_secondary_elaborations: Isaiah's indictments of worship 'in gardens' (Isaiah 1:29-30; 65:3) refer symbolically to Judah trusting in and running to foreign nations rather than to literal pagan cultic groves
Isaiah 66:17 ('in the gardens behind one in the midst') means entering among the nations and following one of them, with the note that 'tree' is a translator-supplied word absent from the Hebrew
The clean/unclean food distinction is eternal because eating swine's flesh remains grounds for judgment at the last-judgment scene of Isaiah 66:15-19
The wider symbol taxonomy: mountain=kingdom, tree=nation, sea=unrooted peoples, grass=individual mortal, beast=nation in its wild aspect
Revelation 7:3's 'hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees' reads as protection of peoples and nations before the sealing
strongest_counter_interpretation: The garden is Eden/paradise — the place of God's ordered, life-giving presence and communion with humanity (Genesis 2-3), lost through sin and restored in Revelation 22. On this reading, Ezekiel 31 uses Eden's garden as the archetype of primeval splendor: Assyria's cedar is so magnificent that even the trees of God's paradise would envy it, a hyperbolic simile drawing on Eden as the standard of created glory, not a statement that the garden itself denotes a collection of nations. Isaiah's 'gardens' passages are then literal pagan cultic groves, a practice well attested historically.
counter_core_identification: Garden = Eden/paradise, the locus of divine presence and blessed communion, framing the canonical arc of paradise created, lost, and restored.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that 'garden' symbolically denotes a grouping of nations; it holds that the garden denotes a place — God's paradisiacal domain and presence — so that in Ezekiel 31 the garden imagery functions only as a splendor comparison to primeval Eden, and in Isaiah the gardens are literal cultic sites, not the nations.
counter_case: Genesis 2:8-15 and 3:8,23-24 establish the garden as the place of divine presence, provision, and lost communion — the foundational usage of the term
Revelation 2:7 and 22:1-5 deliberately return to garden imagery (tree of life, river) to depict restored communion, closing the canonical arc
Isaiah 51:3 and Ezekiel 36:35 compare restored Zion/land to 'the garden of Eden,' treating the garden as a paradigm of blessed place, not a group of nations

Historical-critical scholarship reads Isaiah 1:29, 65:3, and 66:17 as references to actual pagan garden/grove cults, with the ritual details (incense, purification rites, eating swine and mouse) fitting known cultic practice literally

Ezekiel 31 can be read as extended simile: the cedar's greatness is measured against Eden's trees as the gold standard of splendor (31:8-9), so 'garden of God' evokes paradise rather than defining the symbol
book_explanatory_advantages: Ezekiel himself decodes the trees: 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude' (31:18), and Assyria is the cedar (31:3), so the trees of Eden in the garden of God are nations by the prophet's own key — the book needs no added hyperbole step

The trees of Eden are 'comforted in the nether parts of the earth' and go down to Sheol (31:16-17), which is intelligible only if they are kings/nations, not paradise vegetation — the book's reading absorbs this directly

The tree=nation equation is independently established by explicit in-text decodings (Daniel 4:20-22; Ezekiel 17:22-24; Daniel 7:17 for the parallel beast figure), making garden=stand-of-nation-trees a minimal inference

The paradise reading strains to explain heathen empires standing 'in the garden of God' if the garden denotes unbroken divine communion; the book's reading (God plants and fells all nations, Ezekiel 17:24) explains it without tension

The book's reading of Isaiah 66:17 correctly notes that 'tree' is translator-supplied ('after one in the midst' in the Hebrew), and the immediate context (66:18-19) is explicitly about gathering and sending to the nations, which coheres with the national reading
counter_explanatory_advantages: The counter better fits the term's foundational and terminal usages (Genesis 2-3; Revelation 22), which the book's entry does not address at all
Literal garden-cults are historically attested, and the concrete ritual details of Isaiah 65:3-4 and 66:17 (bricks, incense, purification, specific unclean foods) read naturally as actual practice
Isaiah 51:3 and Ezekiel 36:35 use 'garden of Eden' as a simile for restored blessed land, showing the term can function as a paradigm of place rather than a group of nations
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 31:3,9,16-18 (cedar = Assyria; trees of Eden envy him, descend to Sheol; 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude')
Daniel 4:20-22 (the great tree explicitly decoded as the king and his dominion)
Ezekiel 17:22-24 ('all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree' — the trees are the nations God raises and fells)
Isaiah 66:17-19 (gardens passage immediately followed by the gathering of 'all nations and tongues,' with 'tree' absent from the Hebrew text)
unresolved_objections: The Isaiah gardens passages (1:29-30; 65:3; 66:17) may still be literal pagan grove-cults per mainstream historical scholarship; the book's symbolic reading is plausible and context-supported but not conclusively established over the literal one

The entry's definition does not address the term's use in Genesis 2-3, the Song of Songs, or Revelation 22, where the paradise/presence and bridal senses are clearly operative; the book's definition is best treated as governing the prophetic nation-tree contexts rather than every biblical 'garden'
The chapter's doctrinal extension that the clean/unclean food law is eternal goes beyond the symbol's identification and is not required by the entry's core
